title: Ozone, Montreal Protocol and Other Conventions

cards.h: Convention names and years are free marks
cards.b:
Prelims often matches a convention with its subject or year. The Montreal Protocol is also the most cited success story in global environmental governance.

Learn the ozone chain, then the table of conventions.

Prelims often tests pairs such as Basel with hazardous waste, Ramsar with wetlands, and Minamata with mercury. Build a timeline in your head: 1971 Ramsar, 1972 Stockholm and World Heritage, 1973 CITES, 1987 Montreal, 1992 Rio. Also remember that Vienna is the framework and Montreal is the protocol with binding limits.

Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere (peak about 20 to 30 km up) absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C. It is measured in Dobson Units. Ground-level ozone is a pollutant.

Rowland and Molina (1974) warned about CFCs. In 1985 Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin reported the Antarctic ozone hole. Crutzen, Rowland and Molina won the Nobel Prize in 1995.

UV-B can cause skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops and plankton. The ozone hole forms over Antarctica each spring (September to October) because polar stratospheric clouds help chlorine destroy ozone. Remember the contrast: stratospheric ozone is protective, while tropospheric (ground-level) ozone is a pollutant.

CFCs are stable, drift up, and in the stratosphere UV frees chlorine. One chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. The hole forms in the Antarctic spring (September to October) because polar stratospheric clouds help the reaction.

Other ozone depleting substances (ODS): halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, methyl bromide, HCFCs.

The Vienna Convention (1985) set up cooperation. The Montreal Protocol (1987, in force 1989) phases out ODS. It is the first treaty ratified by every country in the world.

It works with a Multilateral Fund to help developing countries, and has binding timetables. Amendments: London (1990), Copenhagen (1992), Montreal (1997), Beijing (1999) and Kigali (2016).

HFCs do not harm ozone but are strong greenhouse gases. The Kigali Amendment (in force 2019) phases them down. India ratified it in 2021.

India’s schedule: freeze in 2028 and cuts in steps, with an 85 percent reduction by 2047, later than developed countries. Scientists project the ozone layer recovering by about 2040 (most of the world), 2045 (Arctic) and 2066 (Antarctic), per UNEP’s 2022 assessment.

• Ramsar 1971: wetlands.
  • World Heritage Convention 1972.
  • CITES 1973: trade in endangered species.
  • CMS 1979 (Bonn): migratory species.
  • CBD 1992 with Cartagena Protocol (2000, biosafety) and Nagoya Protocol (2010, access and benefit sharing).
  • UNCCD 1994: desertification.

The Ramsar and World Heritage conventions protect sites, while CITES and CMS protect species. CBD, adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, has three goals: conservation, sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits. Its Kunming-Montreal framework of 2022 sets global biodiversity goals. UNCCD, also born at Rio, is the only legally binding convention on land.

• Basel 1989: hazardous waste.
  • Rotterdam 1998: prior informed consent for chemicals.
  • Stockholm 2001: persistent organic pollutants.
  • Minamata 2013: mercury (in force 2017).
  • MARPOL 1973/78: ship pollution.
  • BBNJ (High Seas Treaty), adopted 2023 and in force from January 2026.

The Basel Convention covers cross-border movement of hazardous waste. Rotterdam and Stockholm deal with hazardous pesticides and persistent organic pollutants such as DDT. Minamata is named after the Japanese city where mercury poisoning was seen in the 1950s. MARPOL has six annexes covering oil, chemicals, sewage, garbage and air pollution from ships. BBNJ concerns biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

Success factors: clear science, substitutes available, binding timetables, trade restrictions on non-parties, a fund for poor countries and a review system.

Climate change is harder: no easy substitute for fossil fuels, costs are high and benefits are shared. Some argue the Kigali style phase-down model could help other gases.

Montreal's Multilateral Fund helped developing countries pay for the switch, and longer timetables gave India and China more time, reflecting common but differentiated responsibilities. The treaty has been amended several times (London, Copenhagen, Montreal, Beijing and Kigali) so it adjusts to new science. It was the first treaty ratified by every country.

India phased out CFCs by 2010 and has a Ozone Cell in MoEFCC and an HCFC Phase-out Management Plan. India is a party to all the conventions above.

India submitted its 2022 and 2026 climate plans and hosted CMS COP13 (2020) and UNCCD COP14 (2019).

Mains-style: “Montreal Protocol is the most successful environmental treaty. What lessons does it offer for climate change?” Structure: what it did; why it worked; limits of the analogy; Kigali; India’s role.

Prelims tip: Montreal = ozone, 1987. Kigali = HFCs. Basel = hazardous waste. Minamata = mercury. Rotterdam = PIC chemicals.
